qt: to the Commission Marko Vešligaj (S&D) Subject:

The case of Gospić in Croatia, where between 34 000 and 37 000 tonnes of illegally dumped waste were found in one area, shows how serious the long-term consequences of inadequate waste management can be for local communities and the environment. Alongside concerns about potential soil and water contamination, and its consequences for human health and lives, as well as for agricultural production, the question of liability for the costs of waste removal, site remediation and long-term post-remediation monitoring also arises. Regulation (EU) 2021/1060, through thematic condition 2.6, requires updated planning for investments in waste management which, among other things, must identify the investment gap and sources of revenue to cover the infrastructure’s operating and maintenance costs. 1.

Can the Commission clarify whether, in the context of the approval and implementation of cohesion policy investments in waste management in Croatia, it has verified compliance with the thematic condition 2.6, in particular with regard to the long-term financial sustainability of the infrastructure?

Does the Commission consider that, when financing such projects, appropriate mechanisms should be required to cover the costs of landfill closure, remediation and post-closure monitoring, including financial guarantees and adequate landfill fees, in order to avoid the cost of the consequences of inadequate waste management ultimately being borne by citizens and the public purse?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.11.2026) The criteria upon which the Commission assessed the fulfilment of the thematic enabling condition 2.6. ‘Updated planning for waste management’ are laid down in Annex IV of the Common Provision Regulation (CPR)1. The Commission assessed Croatian enabling condition 2.6. as fulfilled on 15 March 20242. As cohesion policy programmes are implemented under shared management, the managing authorities must apply criteria and procedures set out in Article 73 when selecting operations. These include the consistency of operations with the strategies and plans established for the fulfilment of the applicable enabling conditions, as well as their financial sustainability. The current Croatian cohesion policy programmes include measures addressing remediation of non-hazardous waste landfills. In general, the full lifecycle costs of landfill operations should be considered when planning the investments. This includes the costs of closure, remediation where necessary, and post-closure monitoring. In line with the ‘polluter pays’ principle and EU waste legislation, Member States should ensure that landfill charges and other financing arrangements reflect these costs, so that the environmental and financial consequences of inadequate waste management are not shifted to citizens or the public purse. Overall, the Commission is vigilant that EU investments comply with the EU environmental law and the waste hierarchy, with prevention, reuse and recycling and recovery taking priority over disposal.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/1060/oj/eng. 2 More details on the process were provided in the reply to written question E-00389/26;
